account: The ACCESS trial enrolled young people with diabetes at two Johns Hopkins clinics in Baltimore. Of 164 participants randomized, one control was excluded after entering another screening study. All 81 participants assigned to an IDx-DR eye exam completed screening, compared with 18 of 82 controls referred to an eye-care provider. The AI marked 25 results as positive, and 16 of those participants attended an eye-care visit within six months. A retina specialist reviewed all AI images for safety because the device was not cleared for this age group. The study measured screening and follow-up. No source reports vision outcomes for the ACCESS participants. In February 2025 two Johns Hopkins clinicians reported that the system was still in systematic use for youth and adults. In April 2026 reviewers at the University of Oxford and the University of Western Australia, who have no tie to the maker or to Johns Hopkins, rated the ACCESS trial at low risk of bias. They found that its gain in follow-up was the largest of six studies of AI-assisted eye screening. A follow-on Johns Hopkins trial, ACCESS 2, is due to finish at the end of 2026.

ai_role.statement: IDx-DR assessed retinal photographs and returned a screening result during the diabetes visit. The trial compared this on-site service with referral elsewhere. A retina specialist also reviewed the images for safety. A coauthor had financial interests in the manufacturer, although he did not have access to the underlying data.

Turner, Michael Kidd, John Powell and Catherine Pope, Referral uptake after diabetic retinopathy screening with artificial intelligence-assisted care pathways: a systematic review and meta-analysis, npj Digital Medicine 9: 468, 17 April 2026. purpose: IDx-DR/LumineticsCore is built to autonomously detect more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy from fundus images at the point of care. Increasing screening completion is its intended benefit.

ratings.reason: The trial measured a substantial increase in completed diabetic eye exams. It did not establish improved vision or prevention of blindness.

echoes.setting: RAIDERS randomized trial in Rwanda (Mathenge et al., Ophthalmology Science, 2022): immediate AI results at the point of care raised referral uptake to 51.5% against 39.6%, as summarized by Leigh et al. (2026)
